definition: A respectful Filipino title used before the first name of an older or married woman, especially one of the working or vendor class. Unlike the Spanish-derived 'Señora', 'Aling' is native Tagalog in origin and conveys warmth and familiarity rather than formal status.
example: Aling Nena, may pansit po ba kayo ngayon?
exampleTranslation: Mrs. Nena, do you have pansit today?

definition: Literally 'newly arrived'. Used to describe anyone who has just come to town — a stranger, a traveler, or in Ibarra's case, a Filipino returning from years abroad. In a close-knit colonial town like San Diego, a bagong dating is immediately noticed and talked about.
example: Ang bagong dating na iyan ay mula sa Europa, sabi nila.
exampleTranslation: That newcomer is from Europe, they say.

definition: A common adverb of uncertainty, used to express possibility or doubt. Equivalent to 'maybe' or 'might' in English. Often softened with 'po' for politeness when speaking to elders or superiors.
example: Baka po malaon ang inyong pananatili dito.
exampleTranslation: Perhaps your stay here will be a long one.

definition: A respectful title for an unmarried young woman of good family, equivalent to 'Miss' or 'Mademoiselle'. Maria Clara, the beloved of Ibarra, is the archetypal binibini of the Noli — demure, pious, and educated in the convent. The word shares its root with 'babae' (woman) and connotes grace and propriety.
example: Narito po ang Binibining Maria Clara.
exampleTranslation: Miss Maria Clara is here.

definition: A Spanish loanword ('capitán') used in colonial Philippines for the gobernadorcillo (town mayor) or the capitán del barrio (village head). Capitán Tiago, host of Ibarra's homecoming reception, holds such a title. The Spanish honorific reflects three centuries of colonial administration, where local Filipino elites were granted Spanish titles in exchange for loyalty to the Crown.
example: Si Capitán Tiago po ay naghanda ng handaan.
exampleTranslation: Captain Tiago has prepared a feast.

definition: A heartfelt exclamation of shock, distress, or awe. 'Diyos' is the Spanish loanword for God (from 'Dios'), adopted into Filipino during three centuries of Spanish Catholic rule. The phrase reflects the deep Catholic faith woven into everyday Filipino speech — even non-religious contexts invoke the divine.
example: Diyos ko! Anong nangyari sa kanya?
exampleTranslation: My God! What happened to him?

definition: Used alone as an exclamation of praise — 'Excellent!' or 'Well done!' As a noun it means 'skill' or 'origin' (galing sa Maynila = 'from Manila'), and as an adjective it means 'great' or 'skilled'. A versatile word that captures the Filipino value of praising effort and ability.
example: Galing! Napakagaling ng iyong sinabi.
exampleTranslation: Excellent! What you said was very wise.

definition: A respectful Filipino title for a man, equivalent to 'Sir' or 'Mister'. Often paired with the Spanish 'Don' for men of higher social standing. The plural 'mga ginoo' (gentlemen) appears in formal addresses. Native to Tagalog, it predates the Spanish colonial era and survived alongside imported titles like 'Señor'.
example: Mabuhay po, Ginoo. Anong maipaglilingkod ko?
exampleTranslation: Welcome, sir. How may I help you?

definition: The primary Tagalog word for 'no' or 'not'. Note: this is unrelated to the Hindi language of India — a coincidence that surprises many learners. When answering a question negatively, 'hindi' is often repeated or paired with 'po' for politeness: 'Hindi po.'
example: Hindi ko po alam ang sagot.
exampleTranslation: I do not know the answer.

definition: The Tagalog word for 'friend', from the root 'kaibigan' (one who is loved/befriended). Filipino culture places great value on friendship and 'pakikisama' (getting along). A kaibigan is not merely an acquaintance but someone with whom one shares mutual trust and loyalty — a bond often stronger than family ties in the novel's social world.
example: Si Ibarra ay isang matalik na kaibigan ng kanyang ama.
exampleTranslation: Ibarra is a close friend of his father.

definition: Steamed white rice, the staple food of every Filipino meal. 'Bigas' refers to uncooked rice, while 'kanin' is the cooked grain eaten at breakfast, lunch, and dinner. A meal without kanin is hardly considered a meal at all — even breakfast at Capitán Tiago's table would be built around it. Rice cultivation has shaped Filipino life for over 3,000 years.
example: Maraming kanin po tayo ngayong hapunan.
exampleTranslation: We have plenty of rice for tonight's supper.

definition: The standard Filipino daytime greeting, literally 'beautiful day'. 'Maganda' means beautiful or good, and 'araw' means sun or day. It can be made time-specific: 'Magandang umaga' (good morning), 'Magandang tanghali' (good noon), 'Magandang hapon' (good afternoon), 'Magandang gabi' (good evening). Often followed by 'po' to show respect.
example: Magandang araw po, Mang Tenyo.
exampleTranslation: Good day, Mang Tenyo.

definition: A versatile adjective meaning 'good', 'well', or 'fine'. 'Mabuti na' means 'it's better now' or 'good thing'. When asked 'Kumusta ka?' (How are you?), the polite answer is 'Mabuti' (Well). The root word 'buti' also appears in 'kabutihan' (goodness) — a central concept in Filipino moral thought.
example: Mabuti naman po ang aking pakiramdam.
exampleTranslation: I am feeling well.

definition: A Tagalog verb meaning 'to see' or 'to be able to see', from the root 'kita' (see). Filipino verbs use a complex system of affixes (um-, mag-, ma-, -in, i-) to mark aspect and focus. 'Makita' specifically uses the 'ma-' prefix denoting ability — literally 'to be able to see'.
example: Gusto kong makita si Ibarra ng aking sariling mga mata.
exampleTranslation: I want to see Ibarra with my own eyes.

definition: A respectful Filipino title used before the first name of an older or working-class man — the male counterpart of 'Aling'. 'Mang' is a contraction of 'Mangge' or 'Manong' (elder brother). Used for cart drivers, vendors, and laborers, it conveys respect without the formality of 'Ginoo'. Mang Tenyo, the cart driver, is addressed this way throughout Chapter 1.
example: Mang Tenyo, salamat po sa iyong tulong.
exampleTranslation: Mang Tenyo, thank you for your help.

definition: A Tagalog verb meaning 'to hear', from the root 'dinig' (sound/hearing). Used in the gossip scenes of the Noli, where characters strain to overhear conversations not meant for them. 'Marinig' uses the 'ma-' prefix denoting involuntary or potential action — one does not choose to hear; one simply hears.
example: Hindi ko marinig ang kanilang usapan.
exampleTranslation: I could not hear their conversation.

definition: The capital of the Philippines, founded as a Spanish colonial city in 1571 by Miguel López de Legazpi on the site of a pre-colonial Muslim settlement. The name derives from 'May nilad' ('where the nilad flower grows'). In the Noli, Manila is the cosmopolitan center where ilustrados like Ibarra study, merchants trade, and Spanish authority is centered at Intramuros, the walled city.
example: Galing po ako sa Maynila, at dito muna ako tatagal.
exampleTranslation: I come from Manila, and I will stay here for a while.

definition: The standard Tagalog word for 'yes'. Repeated or drawn out ('Oo nga') for emphasis. The polite form is 'Opo', used when speaking to elders or superiors. In colonial society, the choice between 'oo' and 'opo' immediately signaled the speaker's awareness of social hierarchy — a subtlety exploited throughout Rizal's dialogue.
example: Oo po, naririnig ko kayo.
exampleTranslation: Yes, I hear you.

definition: A Spanish loanword meaning both 'father' (parent) and 'Father' (Catholic priest). In the colonial Philippines, the fraile or friar held enormous power — spiritual, political, and economic. Padre Dámaso, the Franciscan antagonist of the Noli, embodies this authority: a single friar could make or unmake a town's fortunes. The word still carries weight today.
example: Ang Padre Dámaso ay galit kay Ibarra.
exampleTranslation: Father Dámaso is angry at Ibarra.

definition: The Filipino word for farewell or goodbye, from the root 'alam' (knowledge/notice) — literally 'to take notice' as a parting gesture. More formal and emotional than the casual 'babay' (from English 'bye'). Used when parting for a long time or forever, as Ibarra parts from his old life in San Diego.
example: Paalam po, Mang Tenyo. Hangang sa muli.
exampleTranslation: Farewell, Mang Tenyo. Until we meet again.

definition: The quintessential Filipino bread roll — slightly sweet, dusted with breadcrumbs, baked in wood-fired ovens. Its name is Spanish ('pan de sal' = 'bread of salt'), though the bread itself is a Filipino adaptation of European breadmaking introduced during the colonial era. Eaten at breakfast, often dipped in coffee, pan de sal remains the most popular bread in the Philippines today.
example: Mainit pa ang pan de sal, gusto niyo po ba?
exampleTranslation: The pan de sal is still warm, would you like some?

definition: A Filipino noodle dish adapted from Chinese Hokkien cuisine (the word 'pansit' or 'pancit' comes from the Hokkien 'pian e sit', meaning 'something conveniently cooked fast'). Chinese traders settled in the Philippines centuries before the Spanish arrived, and pansit is one of their lasting culinary legacies. Different regions have their own varieties — pansit bihon, pansit canton, pansit malabon — served at every fiesta and birthday celebration for long life.
example: Magluluto ako ng pansit para sa handaan bukas.
exampleTranslation: I will cook pansit for tomorrow's feast.

definition: A Tagalog verb meaning 'to go' or 'to travel to', from the root 'punta' (destination/point). Uses the '-um-' infix to mark the actor focus and completed aspect. Movement verbs like this are central to a novel about journeys — Ibarra's return to San Diego, his trips to Manila, and the characters' daily comings and goings through the town plaza.
example: Pumunta siya sa simbahan nang maaga.
exampleTranslation: He went to the church early.

definition: An adverb meaning 'together', 'simultaneously', or 'at the same time'. 'Sabay-sabay' emphasizes a group acting as one. Filipino culture values collective action — bayanihan (communal unity) — and 'sabay' captures this spirit of moving in step with one's neighbors and family.
example: Sabay tayong pumunta sa plaza.
exampleTranslation: Let's go to the plaza together.

definition: The Filipino word for 'thank you', from the root 'salamat' meaning safety or wholeness. The phrase 'salamat po' adds the politeness particle 'po'. 'Maraming salamat' means 'thank you very much' (literally 'much thanks'). The word shares its Arabic root 'salam' (peace) with neighboring Malay and Indonesian cultures — a legacy of pre-colonial trade across the archipelago.
example: Maraming salamat po sa inyong kabutihan.
exampleTranslation: Thank you very much for your kindness.

definition: An all-purpose Filipino interjection borrowed from Spanish 'sigue' (continue/follow). Used to grant permission ('Go ahead'), agree to a request ('OK'), or encourage continuation ('Keep going'). One of the most frequently spoken words in casual Filipino conversation — versatile enough to serve as greeting, assent, and farewell all in one.
example: Sige, sige. Mauna na ako.
exampleTranslation: OK, OK. I'll go on ahead.

definition: Literally 'breasts', used as a mild exclamation of shock, frustration, or surprise — roughly equivalent to 'Good heavens!' or 'For crying out loud!'. A uniquely Filipino expression that sounds crude in literal translation but functions as a relatively tame oath in everyday speech. Often paired with 'Diyos ko' for emphasis.
example: Suso! Ang init naman ngayong araw.
exampleTranslation: Good heavens! It's so hot today.

definition: The Filipino word for gossip, derived from the Spanish 'chisme' (gossip) but pronounced with the characteristic Filipino 'ts' sound. Tsismis is practically a social institution in the Philippines — exchanged over garden fences, at the market, and after Mass. In the Noli, tsismis is how information (and misinformation) travels through San Diego, shaping public opinion about Ibarra, Maria Clara, and the friars.
example: May bagong tsismis daw tungkol sa bagong dating.
exampleTranslation: There's new gossip about the newcomer, they say.

definition: A Tagalog verb meaning 'to leave' or 'to depart', from the root 'alis' (departure). Uses the '-um-' infix marking actor focus and completed aspect. Departure is a recurring theme in the Noli — Ibarra's departure for Europe, his return, and the departures (voluntary and forced) of various characters throughout the novel. The imperative 'Umalis ka!' means 'Leave!' — a sharp command.
example: Umalis si Ibarra nang hindi nagpaalam.
exampleTranslation: Ibarra left without saying goodbye.

definition: The standard Filipino response to 'salamat' (thank you), literally 'nothing at all' or 'it's nothing'. This embodies the Filipino virtue of humility — to deflect gratitude by minimizing one's own contribution. The phrase signals that the kindness given was an obligation of friendship or kinship, not a debt to be repaid.
example: Walang anuman po. Ito ang aking tungkulin.
exampleTranslation: You're welcome. It is my duty.
